title: Pauri 15: trusting, the door of freedom
hook: mannai: by trust one finds the door of liberation and helps others across (Japji 15)

segments.voice: Yesterday, maarag, the road: by trusting, it meets no barrier. Your line was the way opens. Today, the last trusting stanza, and the end of this stretch of the path.

A river, and no bridge yet. Someone who knows the ford wades in, finds the stones, feels the current, and gets to the other side. That's one kind of freedom. But some who cross turn around, wade back, and take a child on their shoulders, then an old man by the arm, then the next one. Getting across is one thing. Carrying others across is another. Pauri 15 ends the trusting stanzas with both.
screen: `A RIVER, NO BRIDGE.` → `ONE WADES ACROSS.` → `THEN TURNS BACK FOR OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Pauri 15, in paraphrase. By trusting, one finds the door of liberation. By trusting, one lifts up one's family. By trusting, the Guru's Sikh crosses over, and carries others across. By trusting, Nanak says, one doesn't wander around begging. And the refrain one last time: such is the Name of the Stainless One, known only to the one who trusts it in the mind. The first line in the original: mannai paavahi mokh duaar. Mokh is the same idea as today's word, mukti: liberation, freedom. Duaar is a door. Indian traditions speak of liberation, and picture it in different ways. Sikh teaching often stresses jivan mukti, being free while alive: here, in a household, with work and family, not only after death or away in a forest. And the very next line lifts the family too. Freedom doesn't pull you out of your people. Then: mannai tarai taare gur sikh. The Guru's Sikh crosses, and carries across. Tarai, crosses over. Taare, makes others cross. The same verb, turned outward. It's the river from the hook, and Sikh scripture comes back to it: the world as a sea, the Name as the boat. The last line, not wandering around begging, is about not having to go door to door for scraps of meaning. That hunger has been met. So the run of eight stanzas lands here. Listen, pauris 8 to 11. Trust, 12 to 15. And trust ends not in private calm but in a door, and in turning back for someone else.
screen: `MOKH DUAAR — THE DOOR OF FREEDOM.` · `FREE WHILE ALIVE, WITH FAMILY.` · `TARAI TAARE — CROSSES, CARRIES.` · `LISTEN, THEN TRUST, THEN CARRY.` · then, large: `FREE, AND FREEING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person stuck on the near bank of something right now: a worry, a task, a hard week. Without solving their whole life, picture one small way you could help them across: a message, a ride, an hour, a listening ear. Hold that picture, then rest with the breath.
Mukti. Liberation, freedom; in Sikh teaching, often freedom while alive. In Pauri 15, the one who trusts finds its door and helps others through.
Your line: free, and freeing. The crossing turns back for others. Day one hundred eighty-six, done.

howItsDone: Pauri 15 closes the four mannai stanzas of Japji Sahib; many Sikhs connect its line about crossing and carrying others across with seva, service to others, as part of daily life.

original.note: Gurmukhi: mukti, liberation; Pauri 15 uses mokh, from the same idea, in mokh duaar, the door of freedom.

trapdoor: what you thought: freedom means getting away from everyone.
what it means: trust opens the door to freedom, lifts your family, and turns you back to help others across.
what a scholar hears: mokh (Sanskrit moksha) duaar, the door of liberation; tarai and taare are one verb, crossing and causing to cross; Sikh teaching stresses jivan mukti.
